pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Repeated tests for reliability (precision vs accuracy)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Working Scientifically — 'measurement'):** Pupils should be taught to understand that whenever a measurement is made there is a source of uncertainty; to make and record observations and measurements using a range of apparatus and methods; and to apply sampling techniques. They use SI units and standard form, choose appropriate instruments with suitable resolution, and evaluate the reliability of methods and suggest improvements.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, grades 6–8):** Students plan investigations that identify what tools are needed, HOW MEASUREMENTS WILL BE RECORDED, and how many data are needed to support a claim; the 9–12 progression makes measurement error and precision explicit. Choosing instrument resolution and considering uncertainty is the 6–8→high-school throughline this topic sits on.

- **Operational details:** The child draws the sharp distinction between PRECISION (how tightly repeated readings agree with each other) and ACCURACY (how close a reading is to the true value) — the two are independent, so data can be precise but inaccurate (tightly clustered but off) or accurate but imprecise (centred on truth but scattered). They record measurements to an appropriate number of significant figures (not more than the instrument justifies) and use standard form where sensible, and they select an instrument whose resolution suits the quantity (a 10 ml measuring cylinder, not a 1-litre jug, for a 5 ml volume) to minimise uncertainty. The classic model is the target: a tight cluster off-centre = precise/inaccurate; a spread centred on the bullseye = accurate/imprecise; tight on the bullseye = both.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early formal, quantitative). This is where 'careful measuring' becomes a theory of measurement quality. Success = explains precision vs accuracy with correct examples of each combination, rounds a measurement to a sensible number of significant figures, and chooses an instrument of appropriate resolution with a stated reason — underpinning KS3 tables/graphs (sig figs on axes) and the systematic-vs-random error analysis in the age-12+ conclusions topic.
bestPractices: Use the target/dartboard model to separate the two axes: spread of the cluster = precision; offset of the cluster from the bullseye = accuracy.
Deliberately teach all four cases — precise+accurate, precise+inaccurate, imprecise+accurate, imprecise+inaccurate — so pupils see the two ideas are independent.
Connect precision to the instrument's resolution and reliability to the number of repeats — different levers on data quality.
Teach significant figures as 'don't claim more certainty than your instrument gives', linking the number of sig figs to the resolution.
Practise instrument selection by resolution: match the finest sensible instrument to the size of the quantity and justify it.
Distinguish random error (reduced by repeats/averaging, shows as spread) from a bias that shifts accuracy (not fixed by averaging) — previewing the KS3 error-analysis topic.
keyRepresentations: Target/bullseye model — cluster spread = precision, cluster offset = accuracy
Four-quadrant grid of precise/imprecise × accurate/inaccurate outcomes
Significant-figures ladder tied to instrument resolution
Instrument-resolution comparison (1-litre jug vs 10 ml cylinder for a 5 ml volume)
Repeat-readings dot-plot showing spread (precision) around a mean, with the true value marked (accuracy)
commonMisconceptions: Believing tightly-agreeing (precise) readings must be correct, ignoring a systematic offset.
Thinking taking more repeats can fix an inaccurate (biased) instrument — repeats reduce spread, not bias.
Quoting far more significant figures than the instrument's resolution justifies (false precision).
Assuming a bigger or more expensive instrument is automatically more precise, regardless of resolution for the quantity.
Treating a single close reading as proof of accuracy without knowing the true value or the spread.

learn.summary: Help 11–12 year-olds separate PRECISION (how tightly repeated readings agree with each other) from ACCURACY (how close readings are to the true value), recognising the two are independent so data can be precise-but-inaccurate, accurate-but-imprecise, both, or neither. Learners record measurements to a justified number of significant figures (no false precision) and use standard form where sensible, choose instruments whose resolution suits the quantity, and understand that averaging repeated readings reduces the effect of random error on the mean but cannot cure a systematic bias.

activities.title: Two Dials target range: pulling precision and accuracy apart
feedback: If a learner claims a tight cluster must be correct, direct them to the offset dial: keep spread tiny and slide the whole cluster away from the bullseye — consistency has not moved it closer to centre.
If a learner expects averaging to fix an off-centre cluster, have them press 'average more shots' and read the average: it stays off-centre, so repeats cannot cure bias.
On the bench, if a learner quotes more decimals than the instrument shows, point to the instrument's resolution and ask what certainty those extra digits falsely imply.

If a learner picks a coarse jug for a small volume, compare the two dot-plots: in this model the coarse-scale instrument gives a wider spread (larger uncertainty) and the fine-resolution one tightens — what matters here is resolution suited to the volume, not the instrument's size or cost.
activities.rationale: A live two-variable model lets learners manipulate spread and offset independently and directly experience that a tightly agreeing set can still be wrong — the exact misconception this topic targets. The 'average more shots' control makes concrete that averaging repeats reduces the effect of random error on the mean but not systematic bias, and the bench ties the abstraction to choosing instrument resolution and recording to justified significant figures and standard form. These are proposed teaching mechanisms rather than tested interventions.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Working Scientifically ('measurement') requires pupils to understand that whenever a measurement is made there is a source of uncertainty, to use SI units, and to choose apparatus with appropriate resolution.

NGSS SEP 3 (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) grades 6–8 requires students to decide what tools are needed, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim; the 9–12 progression makes measurement error and precision explicit.
learnerActions: Face a bullseye target with two separate controls: a SPREAD dial and an OFFSET (bias) dial.
Fire ten shots with spread set high and observe that the shots scatter all over the target.
Turn the spread dial down and watch the shots pull into a tight knot — name this as high precision.
With the knot tight and near centre, nudge the OFFSET dial and watch the whole tight cluster slide off to one side (e.g. top-left) — still tight, but far from the bullseye.
State what you now see: the shots are as consistent as ever (precise) yet completely off-target (inaccurate), so one dial cannot fix the other.

Press an 'average more shots' / 'take more repeats' button and observe that the individual shots scatter just as much as before (the spread dial sets that), but the average of the shots settles more steadily — and it settles off-centre, not on the bullseye.
Build all four cases deliberately: precise+accurate, precise+inaccurate, imprecise+accurate, imprecise+inaccurate.
Flip to a measurement bench: choose a measuring instrument (coarse jug vs 10 ml cylinder), take repeats, and watch the dot-plot spread relative to a true value that is hidden then revealed.
Record each reading to a justified number of significant figures — not more than the instrument's resolution allows — and use standard form where the value is very large or very small.
Set the cylinder as mis-calibrated and observe that repeats cluster tightly on the wrong value — precise but biased.
activities.intendedInsight: Precision and accuracy are two independent properties of a data set: spread of the cluster shows precision, offset of the cluster from the true value shows accuracy. Taking more repeats does not tighten the spread of individual readings, but averaging them reduces the effect of random error on the mean; it can never remove a systematic bias.

activities.title: Four targets reference: labelling the four cases
feedback: If a learner labels the scattered-but-centred target 'inaccurate', point to where the readings average: spread does not by itself make a set inaccurate.
If a learner labels the tight-off-centre target 'accurate', ask where the bullseye is relative to the cluster — agreement is not closeness to truth.
activities.rationale: A static annotated reference gives a stable explanatory anchor for the four cases and the vocabulary; it complements, rather than replaces, hands-on manipulation of spread and offset. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated resource.
learnerActions: Study four bullseye diagrams, one for each combination: precise+accurate (tight on the bullseye), precise+inaccurate (tight but off-centre), imprecise+accurate (scattered but centred on the bullseye), imprecise+inaccurate (scattered and off-centre).
For each target, state in your own words why it fits that label before revealing the explanation.
Reveal a lift-the-flap explanation on each target (e.g. 'precise + inaccurate: tight but off-centre — why?') and compare it to your reasoning.
Use a linked panel that connects spread → random error (affected by instrument resolution and technique), number of repeats → how reliably the average is pinned down, and offset → systematic bias.
activities.intendedInsight: Each of the four precision/accuracy combinations can be read directly off a target: spread tells you precision, position of the cluster relative to the centre tells you accuracy.

activities.title: Classify real repeated-reading sets
feedback: If a learner calls Amir accurate because his readings agree, contrast agreement with closeness-to-true: his tight cluster sits ~5 g from the real value, so he is precise, not accurate.

If a learner judges Bea by her single reading of exactly 100.0, redirect to the whole set: Bea's mean (100.0 g) is accurate, but her readings scatter up to 0.4 g either side, whereas Cara's mean (about 100.0 g) is also accurate and every reading is within 0.1 g — so Cara is both accurate and precise, while Bea is accurate but less precise.

If a learner says more decimal places or more repeats make a reading more accurate, clarify that significant figures show instrument resolution, and averaging repeats only reduces the effect of random (not systematic) error on the mean — neither fixes a bias.
activities.rationale: Sorting genuine numeric data forces independent judgement of spread versus closeness-to-truth, and Amir's consistent-but-wrong set discriminates learners who conflate the two from those who hold them apart. This is a proposed diagnostic activity, not a tested instrument.
learnerActions: Read three students' five repeated weighings of the same 100.0 g mass: Amir gets 95.1, 95.0, 95.2, 95.1, 95.0 g; Bea gets 100.3, 99.6, 100.4, 99.7, 100.0 g; Cara gets 100.1, 100.0, 99.9, 100.0, 100.1 g.
Decide whose readings are precise, whose are accurate, and whose are both, and write the reason for each.
Explain in your own words what 'precise' and 'accurate' each mean, using these results as evidence.
Explain why Amir's readings are the tricky case — consistent yet consistently wrong.
Answer: what could make Amir's readings consistently 5 g low, and would taking more repeats fix it?
Answer: if you had to trust one person's method, whose would you pick, and why?
Answer: you need to measure 5 ml of liquid — would you choose a 1-litre jug or a 10 ml cylinder, and why?
Judge whether writing a weighing as 95.13 g is justified, and say what that extra decimal place wrongly implies.
activities.intendedInsight: Amir is precise but not accurate (readings close to each other but all ~5 g from 100.0 — a systematic error); Bea is accurate on average but not precise (wide scatter averaging near 100.0); Cara is both. Precision is agreement of repeats; accuracy is closeness to the true value; significant figures reflect instrument resolution, not accuracy.

activities.title: Predict-observe: the zero-error balance
feedback: If a learner predicted 'they'll agree, so they'll be right (100 g)', revisit the zero error: the balance started 5 g high, so every reading carries the same offset and all land on 105 g.
If a learner expects more repeats to fix it, point out that every reading shares the identical bias — averaging many 105 g readings still gives 105 g.
activities.rationale: A commit-then-observe surprise where consistent readings are consistently wrong confronts the precision/accuracy conflation directly and distinguishes systematic from random error. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Watch as a balance is set to read 5 g with nothing on the pan (an uncorrected zero error), and confirm it does this consistently.
Before any weighing, predict what five repeated weighings of a known 100 g mass will read, and whether those readings will be accurate — commit to a reason in writing.
Observe the five actual readings (the balance reads a consistent 105 g every time).
Compare your prediction with the result and explain what the outcome shows about precision versus accuracy.
Decide whether taking even more repeats would bring the readings closer to 100 g, and justify your answer.
activities.intendedInsight: A consistent, repeatable reading (high precision) can still be systematically wrong (low accuracy); repeating a measurement does not remove a systematic error such as an uncorrected zero offset.

activities.title: In-role technician reasoning check (optional companion)
feedback: If a learner answers that agreeing readings must be right, ask them to name a situation (e.g. a mis-set balance) where all readings agree yet are all wrong.
Pair this discussion with a target or dot-plot visual so claims about spread and offset can be checked against a picture.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning surfaces and tests the learner's reasoning and is well suited to eliciting justification; it works best alongside a visual model so learners can see the clusters they are describing. Proposed as a companion, not a standalone or tested method.
learnerActions: Respond to an in-role 'lab technician' who poses probing scenarios, e.g. 'your three readings agree beautifully — does that make them right?'
Explain aloud or in writing whether agreement between readings guarantees closeness to the true value, and why not.
Reason through a case where readings are scattered but centred on the true value and say what that reveals about precision and accuracy.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the distinction in response to challenge consolidates that agreement (precision) and closeness-to-truth (accuracy) are separate claims about a data set.

constraints: Recognition and sorting tasks (categorising target diagrams, multiple-choice 'precise or accurate?', fill-in-the-blank rounding, matching quantities to instruments) assess whether the two concepts are held apart but do not themselves elicit the independent manipulation of spread and offset through which the independence is discovered; use them to check understanding, not as the sole route to building it.
A static annotated target is a strong explanatory reference but does not let the learner vary spread and bias themselves; treat it as a companion to hands-on or observed manipulation.
An in-role conversation is a reasoning check, not a substitute for seeing clusters move; pair it with a visual model rather than using it standalone.

Any claim about instrument calibration or instrument behaviour depends on the specific instrument and setup; use the mis-calibrated-cylinder and zero-error-balance examples as concrete illustrations, not universal rules.

Significant figures indicate instrument resolution, not accuracy; do not let learners treat extra decimals as making a reading more accurate, or extra repeats as removing a systematic bias (averaging repeats only reduces the effect of random error on the mean).
A bigger or more expensive instrument is not automatically more precise; precision for a given quantity depends on resolution suited to that quantity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.

Restored 'standard form where sensible' to the summary and the bench recording step; the original objective/description explicitly requires using significant figures AND standard form, and the earlier candidate had dropped standard form entirely.

Self-audit of the numeric example: Amir's set (95.1, 95.0, 95.2, 95.1, 95.0 for a 100.0 g mass) is tightly clustered ~5 g low → precise, not accurate; Bea's (100.3, 99.6, 100.4, 99.7, 100.0) is widely scattered with mean = 100.0 → accurate on average, not precise; Cara's (100.1, 100.0, 99.9, 100.0, 100.1) is tight and centred (mean ≈100.02) → both. These classifications are internally consistent and retained as given.

Self-audit of the zero-error PoE: a balance reading 5 g with an empty pan adds a constant +5 g offset, so a true 100 g mass reads a consistent 105 g — consistent with the stated outcome and correctly illustrating that repeats do not remove a systematic offset.

The source labels the 2D interactive 'ideal' and rates 3D as adding 'no conceptual gain' and the quiz as unable to 'deliver the two-dial manipulation'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims; they have been reframed as scoped affordances/limits (recognition tasks assess rather than elicit construction) rather than universal laws, and no claim of comparative superiority is asserted.

The 'precise but inaccurate' misconception is described in a source as 'dismantled by manipulation'; this is softened to a proposed mechanism, since the sources do not establish that manipulation uniquely defeats the misconception.

Corrected an inherited constraint that referenced 'shade' and 'mesh' (neither appears in this measurement-reliability topic); it is rescoped to instrument calibration/behaviour, and no shade/mesh language remains anywhere in the learner-facing guidance.

assess.poeTask: Set a balance so it reads 5 g with nothing on the pan (an uncorrected zero error). Show the child it's consistent, then ask them to predict what five repeated weighings of a known 100 g mass will read, and whether those readings will be accurate — commit to a reason. Many predict 'they'll agree, so they'll be right (100 g).' The balance reads a consistent 105 g every time. Consistent-but-wrong forces apart precision (the readings agree) from accuracy (they're all 5 g too high), and shows repeats don't remove a systematic error.
probeDeeper: What could make Amir's readings consistently 5 g low? Would taking more repeats fix it?
If you had to trust one person's method, whose would you pick, and why?
You need to measure 5 ml of liquid — would you choose a 1-litre jug or a 10 ml cylinder, and why?
Amir writes 95.13 g. Is that extra decimal place justified? What does it wrongly imply?
assess.correctAnswer: Amir is precise but not accurate (readings very close to each other but all far from 100.0 — a systematic error). Bea is accurate on average but not precise (readings scatter widely, though they average near 100.0). Cara is both precise and accurate (tightly grouped AND close to 100.0). Precision is how close repeated readings are to each other; accuracy is how close they are to the true value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Precision/accuracy conflation: 'Amir is accurate because his readings all agree' — treats consistency as correctness.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast agreement with closeness-to-true; show Amir's tight cluster sits 5 g away from the real value — precise, not accurate.
errorPatterns.distractor: Amir's readings are accurate because they're all so close together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tier-1 labels Amir accurate; Tier-2 justifies it by how close his readings are to each other, not to 100.0.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accuracy = one lucky reading: picks the single value nearest 100.0 as 'the accurate one' rather than judging the set.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Judge accuracy from the whole set's closeness to true (e.g. the mean), not a single fortunate reading.
errorPatterns.distractor: Bea is the most accurate because one of her readings hit exactly 100.0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names Bea most accurate because one reading hit exactly 100.0.

errorPatterns.pattern: More decimals / more repeats = more accurate: thinks extra significant figures, or simply repeating more, makes a reading more accurate rather than revealing precision or averaging random error.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Significant figures show instrument resolution, not accuracy; repeats reduce random (not systematic) error — they can't fix a bias.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When discussing significant figures or repeats, equates them with accuracy.

responseLevels.gap: Calls Amir accurate because his readings agree; treats consistent as correct, or picks a single close reading as 'accurate'.
responseLevels.full: Correctly classifies all three (precise-not-accurate, accurate-not-precise, both), explains precision as agreement of repeats and accuracy as closeness to the true value, and connects these to systematic vs random error, instrument resolution, and appropriate significant figures.
responseLevels.partial: Defines precision and accuracy separately and labels the clear cases, but stumbles on Amir (consistent-but-wrong), or can't explain that repeats fix random rather than systematic error.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Three students each measure the same 100.0 g mass five times. Amir gets 95.1, 95.0, 95.2, 95.1, 95.0 g. Bea gets 100.3, 99.6, 100.4, 99.7, 100.0 g. Cara gets 100.1, 100.0, 99.9, 100.0, 100.1 g. Whose readings are precise, whose are accurate, and whose are both? Explain what 'precise' and 'accurate' each mean, using their results.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Amir's case is the discriminator — consistent readings that are consistently WRONG. A child who conflates the two (thinks consistent = correct) calls Amir accurate; only someone who separates precision (agreement) from accuracy (closeness to truth) correctly labels Amir precise-but-inaccurate.
